en: The Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya, Scroll One,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha during the Chen Dynasty.
Because one is oppressed by the three kinds of suffering, one desires to know the cause for their cessation.
Seeing that [the argument] is useless and not so, because it is neither certain nor ultimate,
this verse on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is spoken. Formerly, there was a seer named Kapila.
From emptiness arise the four natural virtues:
first, Dharma; second, wisdom; third, freedom from desire; and fourth, mastery. These four together constitute the body.
Beholding this world submerged in blind darkness, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
"Alas! Birth and death exist within blinding darkness.
Surveying the world everywhere, he saw a brahmin of the Aśvalāyana clan.
The deity of the Thousand-Year Shrine concealed his form and went there, speaking these words:
"Asura, this is the way of those who play at staying at home.
Having finished saying this, he immediately returned.
When a thousand years had passed, he returned once more and spoke as before.
The Brahmin then replied to the seer, saying,
"World-Honored One, I truly delight in the ways of a householder."
At that time, having heard this, the seer departed again.
Later, he came once more and spoke the same words as before.
The brahmin answered him in the same manner.
The rishi asked, "Are you able to dwell purely in the holy life?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "I am indeed able to dwell so.
He then abandoned the household life, practiced the conduct of a renunciant, and became a disciple of Kapila.
The outsider asked: "By what causes is this Brahmin born?
He replied: "Because he is oppressed by the three kinds of suffering.
"What are these three sufferings?"
First, based on the internal; second, based on the external; third, based on the celestial.
Regarding that which is based on the internal: it means that because wind, heat, and phlegm are in disharmony, they are able to produce the suffering of illness.
As stated in medical treatises, from the navel downward is called the locus of wind.
From the heart downward is called the "heated region.
From the heart upward, all parts belong to the "neutral" (mild) category.
Sometimes, when the wind element increases and presses upon the neutral and heated regions, wind disorders arise.
The same applies to heat and cold; these are called physical suffering (*kāyika-duḥkha*).
As for mental suffering (*caitasika-duḥkha*), it arises from separation from the beloved, encounter with the hated, and not obtaining what one seeks.
By discriminating these three, mental suffering is produced.
Such suffering as this is called suffering based on the internal.

Suffering based on the external refers to the suffering produced by worldly beings, birds, beasts, venomous snakes, mountain collapses, and the splitting of riverbanks; this is termed external suffering.
Suffering dependent on celestial beings refers to cold, heat, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and so forth;
when one loses their mind due to being thus afflicted by various such celestial disturbances, it is called suffering dependent on celestial beings.
Because one is oppressed by the three types of suffering,
one seeks to know the cause for the cessation of suffering within the realm of desire.
The opponent says:
Because suffering can extinguish these three types of suffering, they are clearly manifested:
first, the eightfold medical prescriptions taught by physicians can extinguish physical suffering;
second, the six desirable sense objects can extinguish mental suffering.
Since this cause has already been revealed,
why do you wish to know it further?
He replied:
This meaning is not non-existent, yet it entails two kinds of faults. Therefore,
if one wishes to know how it does not contradict reason,
those two faults are as follows:
First, there is no fixed limit;
second, there is no ultimate end.
The outsider says:
If the eightfold medical sciences and the like are insufficient as causes for the cessation of suffering because they possess two faults,
then there exists a distinct cause within the four Vedas;
the attainment of results through this cause is certain and ultimate.
Therefore, if you wish to know this, there is no further need [for inquiry].
It is stated within the four Vedas:
"In the past, because I drank the essence of Soma, I attained immortality."
Having attained entry into the realm of the Ābhāsvara devas, one perceives all the devas.
What more can those who are bitter enemies do to me?
And what power does a dead person have over me?
The answer is:
You perceive and hear according to your own biases, which results in the faults of turbidity and inferiority;
however, because I know the nature of excellence and transformation through the reversal of these two causes, [I am not so].
Regarding the "seen cause," that which is explained in medical treatises possesses the faults of being indeterminate and not ultimate.
Regarding the "heard cause," it is obtained through hearsay,
transmitted from Brahmā down to the sages.
Therefore, it is said that the four Vedas are named "according to what is heard.
These Vedas likewise have two faults.
Furthermore, such medical treatises have three faults.
First is impurity. As it is said in the *Piṭaka*:
"O beast, your parents and all your kinsmen rejoice in you."
If you now cast off this body, you will surely be reborn in the heavens.
As it is said in the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice:
"Slaying six hundred animals completely."
If one lacks six hundred of the animal features by three, one cannot be born in heaven for the five matters such as play.
If a person speaks false speech, the devas and rishis declare that this is not a sin.
Such offenses as these exist within the causes according to how they are heard;
therefore, it is not pure.
Second, regarding "falling away":
As it is said in the Vedas:
"For no other reason, Śakra and the Asura kings were destroyed by the power of time."
Because the time cannot be avoided,
if this Dharma were to perish and be extinguished,
the donor would fall from the heavens.
Therefore, there is the sense of falling away.
Third, regarding superiority and inferiority:
it is like a poor person who feels distress upon seeing the wealthy.
The same applies to the ugly and the beautiful, as well as the foolish and the wise; it is likewise with those afflicted by sorrow.
It is also thus among the gods:
those of inferior grade perceive the superior excellence of others and consequently give rise to sorrow and affliction.
Therefore, there is superiority and inferiority.
These three, along with the previous two, are not caused by the Vedas due to these five faults.
The opponent asks:
"If that is so, what is the reason for its superiority?
The respondent answers:
The superiority of these two causes is the reverse:
namely, that the two causes are, first, those taught in medical treatises,
and second, those taught in the Vedas.
To understand the cause obtained by reversing these two causes,
this cause possesses five virtues:
first, it is stable.
Second, the ultimate;
third, purity;
fourth, non-retrogression.
There are five types of equality;
therefore, it is superior to the previous two.
The opponent says:
By what cause is this obtained?
The answer is:
because I know the nature of transformation.
The transformations are two:
first, the great [ego];
second, the ego of self-conceit.
Three and five are the objects;
four and five are the faculties;
five and five are the bases of knowledge.
The six consciousnesses and the five great elements—
these seven are called "transformations" because they are produced by the creative activity of their own nature.
Self-nature (*svabhāva*) is the unchanging primal cause;
the self (*ātman*) is the knower.
When people realize these twenty-five realms of reality, neither increasing nor decreasing them, they will certainly be liberated from the three types of suffering.
As it is said in a verse within the *Vimukti*:
"If one knows that [the self] dwells in any of the twenty-five locations or along any of the paths,
whether wearing matted hair, a topknot, or being shaven-headed, one will attain liberation without doubt."
The outsider asks:
"How are the fundamental nature, its transformation, and the knower distinguished?
He replies:
The fundamental nature is without transformation;
the great elements and so forth are also fundamentally transforming;
the sixteen [derived elements] are merely transformations.
The knower does not undergo fundamental transformation.
That which is the fundamental nature (prakṛti) is capable of producing all things and does not arise from anything else;
therefore, it is called the fundamental nature.
The fundamental nature can give rise to the great elements and so forth;
therefore, it receives the name "fundamental," because it does not arise from anything else.
Therefore, they are not transformations.
The great ego and the five sense objects—
these seven are both the fundamental and the transformed.
Mahat is a transformation because it arises from primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
it is the "root" because it can produce the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*).
Ego-consciousness is a transformation because it arises from Mahat.
It is called "fundamental" because it can produce the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*);
since the seeds of the five subtle elements arise from *ahaṃkāra*, they are "transformations.
It is called "fundamental" because it can produce the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*).
Sound, being merely a seed, gives rise to the emptiness of space and the ear-faculty; thus it serves as the basis.
This continues until fragrance, being merely a seed, gives rise to the earth-element and the nose-faculty.
Thus, these seven are both fundamental and subject to transformation;
the sixteen are subject only to transformation—
namely, the five great elements such as space, the five faculties such as the ear, the five functions such as the tongue, the faculty of the organ, and the mind.
These sixteen dharmas arise only from others;
because they do not give rise to others, they merely undergo transformation.
One who knows this is not originally different [from them].
The "knower" is designated here as the self (*ātman*) because its essence is knowing.
This self is incapable of arising and does not arise from another;
because it differs from the three [preceding categories], it is neither original nor subject to transformation.
The opponent says:
By what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are these three meanings known?
In the world, there are means of valid cognition by which things are known, such as scales, measuring rods, and so forth.
To know length, shortness, lightness, and heaviness.
He replied: "Through direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture."
Because they can penetrate all objects,
there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The establishment of objects depends upon these valid cognitions.
In this treatise, there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The first is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for direct perception:
This wisdom arises from the faculties and their objects and cannot be manifested;
it is neither indeterminate nor dualistic.
This is called valid cognition through realization (*pramāṇa*).
The second is inference (*anumāna*).
As for inference, it is preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Inference is of three kinds:
first, that which has a preceding [perception];
second, that which has a remainder.
Third is impartiality.
Third is the noble speech.
As for "noble speech":
If one relies solely on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), this meaning cannot be understood;
it is only through the authority of the sacred word (*āptāgama*) that it becomes intelligible.
For example, the celestial realms and Uttarakuru are not known through direct perception or inference.
It can be known by means of faith in the noble words.
As for the "noble words," as it is said in a verse:
The Āgamas are the words of the Noble Ones.
The Noble Ones have extinguished all delusions;
being free from delusion, they do not speak falsely.
Because they do not arise from causes and conditions,
they universally pervade all objects.
If there were any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or any other objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), they would not transcend these three meanings.
The six measures of equality are subsumed within authoritative scripture (*āgama*).
Regarding the establishment of objects based on these measures:
"objects" refers to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), as they encompass all things.
Regarding the establishment [of these categories]:
it clarifies why these twenty-five are designated as "objects" (*viṣaya*).
Because they are the objects of the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are established as objects.
Based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), they are briefly established as three; in detail, there are twenty-five.
The opponent says:
It is taught that there are three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). What are the characteristics of these means of valid cognition?
Answer: Direct perception is the cognition that arises in relation to an object;
inference is the threefold distinct cognition.
The characteristic is preceded by the characterized;
the sacred teaching is called "holy word";
and that which understands an object is direct valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The ear gives rise to cognition regarding sounds,
and so on up to the nose giving rise to cognition regarding odors;
yet, cognition alone cannot know.
This is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Regarding the three types of inference (*anumāna*),
the first is that which has a prior [perception].
The second is "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa),
and the third is "equality" (samatā).
These three types of knowledge are so called because they are based on direct valid cognition (pramāṇa).
That which is able to discern these three types of objects as well as the three periods of time is called inference (*anumāna*).
It is like a person who sees black clouds.
One should know that rain will certainly fall.
For example, when one sees the river filled with newly turbid water,
one should know that there must be rain upstream.
Just as one sees the *āmra* trees in the kingdom of Pāṭala put forth flowers,
one should know that it is likewise so in the kingdom of Kośala.
That which has signs is preceded by signs.
The characteristic and that which possesses the characteristic are associated and not separate;
because this characteristic is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) is thereby established.
The "Holy Teaching" (āgama) is called "Holy Word" (āptavacana),
such as the four Vedas and the authoritative treatises spoken by Brahmā and King Manu.
An outsider asks:
It is said that there are three types of inference (*anumāna*).
What are their respective measures and objects? How do they achieve the thorough realization of the means of cognition and its object?
Answer: It is established by means of inference based on equality (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa-anumāna*) that [the object] transcends the domain of the senses.
If the basis of comparison is not manifest,
it appears according to the authoritative word (āptavāda).
This refers to that which relies on equal means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This means that within inference (anumāna), it is called "equal valid cognition" (sama-pramāṇa).
Because both intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and the self (ātman) transcend the senses, they are equally distinguished by this [inference].
The various derivatives, such as the great elements, possess three kinds of qualities:
first, pleasure;
second, suffering.
Third is the darkness of delusion.
If these derivative qualities are separated from their fundamental qualities,
the derivative qualities cannot be established.
Therefore, by inferring the fundamental from the derivative qualities,
the self (ātman) must necessarily exist, as its intrinsic nature is established through the analogy of equality.
Because the great elements and so forth undergo transformation for the sake of others,
the self is also established by way of equality,
provided one relies upon direct perception and inference.
The claim that [this] meaning cannot be established is incorrect,
because it falls outside of knowledge; rather,
one attains understanding by relying on the sacred word.
Just as with the celestial Śakra above, Uttarakuru to the north, and so forth.
The opponent says:
Because intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the self (*ātman*) are not invisible.
Just as the Lord (Īśvara) does not have two heads or three hands,
the answer is:
in reality, there are eight kinds of objects that are invisible.
What are these eight?
They are shown by verse:
"The most distant and the nearest, the impaired faculties and the unsettled mind."
Because they are subtle, obscured, suppressed, overwhelming, similar, aggregated,
or because they are distant from worldly objects that actually exist,
they cannot be perceived; for example, one who has fallen to the other shore cannot perceive this [shore].
Because it is too near, it cannot be seen;
just as when dust is in the eye, one cannot perceive it.
It is not seen because the sense organ is impaired.
It is like a deaf or blind person who cannot perceive sound or form;
because the mind is not concentrated, one does not see.
For example, when the mind is directed toward other objects, it cannot apprehend this particular object.
It is not seen because it is subtle;
just as smoke, heat, dust, or vapors dispersed in the air are not perceived due to their subtlety.
It is also not seen because it is obstructed.
For example, objects outside a wall are concealed and thus cannot be known;
they are not seen because they are obstructed and covered.
For example, when the sunlight appears, the stars and moon no longer manifest.
Because they are similar, they are not seen;
just as a single grain of bean in a heap of beans is difficult to discern due to its similarity to the others,
so too these eight kinds of substantially existent things are invisible.
Furthermore, non-existence is of four kinds and is likewise unknowable.
First, it is invisible prior to arising,
like clay before it has been fashioned into a vessel.
The vessel, however, cannot be known.
Because it has been destroyed and no longer exists, it is not perceived;
just as once a jar has been shattered, it can no longer be known.
Third, it is not seen because of mutual absence,
as for example one does not see a horse within a cow, nor a cow within a horse.
Fourth, it is not seen because of absolute non-existence.
Just as a non-autonomous person does not possess two heads or three hands,
so too these twelve kinds of existence and non-existence cannot be seen. Therefore,
you claim that because they are invisible, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the self (*ātman*) do not exist.
This argument is not tenable.
The opponent says:
If you claim that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the self (*ātman*) are invisible, [then...]
Among the twelve [bases], which one is invisible?
The answer is:
it is invisible for one reason.
What is the single causal condition?
It is shown by verse:
Because its nature is subtle, it is not seen; Yet it is not that which can be seen without a causal condition.
The "great" and so forth are the objects; they do not resemble their nature, yet they resemble it because their nature is subtle and thus imperceptible.
It is not that they lack an objective basis; rather, that which can be seen exists as a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is subtle, it is not seen. For example,
just as smoke and the like, when dispersed in the air, cannot be seen because they are fine,
so too is its intrinsic nature.
It is not like the second head or the third hand, which, being ultimately non-existent, cannot be seen.
The opponent says:
"If it cannot be seen,"
How is it known that existence exists?
The answer is:
because one perceives its own causes and its own nature as produced through conditions.
Based on the equality of the object, one knows through inference that its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) truly exists.
The opponent asks: "What is this object?"
Answer: The "Great Ones" (*mahat*) and so forth are the effects;
from the primal nature (*svabhāva*), the Great One arises.
From Mahat arises the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
from the ego-sense arise the five subtle elements (tanmātras);
from the five subtle elements arise the sixteen manifestations (ṣoḍaśaka).
Since objects such as the Great One (mahat) possess the three qualities (guṇas),
it is known that the primal nature (prakṛti) also possesses the three qualities.
That which resembles [the effect] is not dissimilar to its nature.
This matter is of two kinds:
first, that which is dissimilar to its own nature;
second, that which is similar to its own nature.
For example, suppose a man fathers two sons;
one resembles his father, while the other does not.
This is because phenomena may resemble their original source or not resemble their original source;
this shall be explained in detail later.
This treatise contains such matters as these.
If the disciple is compliant, [one should consider] whether [the self-nature and so forth] exist, do not exist, both exist and do not exist, or neither exist nor do not exist.
Why is this? Because the noble ones' graspings differ.
There are certain noble ones who claim that things such as vases already exist within aggregates of earth and so forth;
the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain the view that these exist after having previously not existed.
That which was taught by Śākyamuni, however, is that within an aggregate of earth, the vase neither exists nor does it not exist.
Based on these three explanations,
it follows that the grasping at a self is the intermediate [state]. He replied:
I shall first refute the tenets of the Śākyas,
and afterwards those of the Vaiśeṣikas.
What the Śākyas teach is neither existent nor non-existent.
This interpretation is incorrect,
for it contradicts itself;
if something does not exist, it follows that it is non-existent.
If it were not non-existent, it would be existent;
for existence and non-existence are contradictory in a single locus,
and thus [the position] cannot be established.
For example, if someone were to say that this person both dies and lives,
such contradictory words would not be established.
The words of Śākyamuni are likewise.
The Tripitaka Master said:
"This calculation is not correct. Why is this so?"
Because Śākyamuni is free from such attachments,
when he says "it is not existent," he does not cling to non-existence;
when he says "it is not non-existent," he does not cling to existence.
Because it is free from the grasping at existence and non-existence, this does not constitute a refutation.
Now, I shall refute the erroneous grasping of the Vaiśeṣika school.
Within the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of the self (*ātman*), there are five reasons.
This demonstrates that the effect definitely exists within the cause.
There are five reasons for this:
because that which does not exist cannot be produced; and because one must necessarily take up the cause.
Because all things are unarisen; because there is the agent and the acted-upon;
because the fruit exists in accordance with its cause; therefore it is said that the fruit exists within the cause.
There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be produced.
In this world, if a thing lacks the conditions for its production, it cannot be accomplished—
just as oil cannot be produced from sand. However,
if a thing possesses the conditions for its production, it can be made— just as oil is extracted from sesame seeds by pressing them.
If a thing does not exist within something,
it cannot emerge from it; yet we now observe that "Greatness" (mahat) and the other principles arise from Primordial Nature (prakṛti).
Therefore, it is known that intrinsic nature possesses greatness and so forth.
Regarding the second point, "because one must necessarily grasp the cause": if a person desires to seek out an object, [they must first grasp its cause].
One must take the cause for obtaining an object.
For example, suppose a person thinks, "Since a Brahmin is expected to come to my house to eat tomorrow, I shall now take some milk.
If there were no butter or curd in the milk, why would he not instead take water?
Because one seeks objects by grasping at causes,
we know that "Greatness" (mahat) exists within the intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Third, because nothing arises from anything.
If the effect were not present within the cause,
then everything would be able to produce all things;
even grass, sand, stones, and the like would be able to produce gold, silver, and other such objects.
This matter is not without cause;
therefore, one knows that the effect exists within the cause.
Fourth, because there is the capacity for the agent and the object acted upon.
For example, just as a potter, fully equipped with his tools, fashions jars, basins, and the like from a mound of clay,
rather than from grass, wood, or other materials, we know that the primal nature (svabhāva) is capable of producing the great elements (mahābhūta) and so forth.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature possesses [qualities] such as magnitude and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the five results exist according to their causes," this means that they follow the specific category of their respective causes.
The same applies to the seed of the fruit.
For example, a barley sprout must necessarily follow from the barley seed;
if the effect were not present within the cause, [it could not arise].
The fruit must necessarily not resemble its cause;
otherwise, sprouts of beans and the like would arise from barley seeds.
Since this is not the case, [the cause and effect must differ].
Therefore, we know that the effect exists because of the cause.
The assertion of the Vaiśeṣikas and others— that the effect does not exist within the cause— is incorrect.
Therefore, it is known that the effect definitely exists within the cause.
The intermediate inquiry is now concluded;
we shall return to continue explaining the preceding meaning.
Regarding those that do not resemble their nature,
there are nine ways in which they do not resemble it:
having a cause, being impermanent, being manifold, being non-pervasive, having an object, and undergoing cessation.
That which has parts, depends on others, undergoes transformation, differs from its own nature,
and is singular— all these have causes.
From the "great" [elements] up to the five great elements, all possess causes.
The primal nature (prakṛti) is the cause of the Great One (mahat);
the Great One is the cause of the I-principle (ahaṃkāra);
and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) have the I-principle as their cause.
Regarding the sixteen entities, such as the sense faculties,
the five *tanmātras* serve as their causes;
their own nature (*svabhāva*) is not so.
Because they do not arise from causes,
they are said to be dissimilar.
Second, regarding impermanence:
The great elements and so forth arise from their intrinsic nature;
because they arise, they are impermanent.
Impermanence is of two kinds.
First, impermanence as abiding for a moment;
second, impermanence as moment-to-moment change.
Regarding impermanence as abiding for a moment:
When it encounters contrary conditions in the future,
it then abides momentarily,
like mountains, trees, and so forth.
When no fire calamity has yet occurred,
it remains stationary for a time;
but if a fire calamity should arrive, [it will be destroyed].
At that time, the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) dissolve into the five subtle elements (tanmātras);
the five subtle elements dissolve into the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The ego-sense dissolves into the Great;
the Great dissolves into primordial nature (prakṛti).
Therefore, the Great and the other principles are impermanent.
The intrinsic nature is not like this,
because it is eternally without cessation.
Third, regarding "many":
That is to say, "greatness" and so forth constitute many persons,
because persons are not identical;
the same applies to pride and the other [defilements].
The intrinsic nature is solely one,
because it is common to many persons.
Regarding the four that are not pervasive:
The self-nature and the self pervade all places—
namely, earth, space, heaven,
and the great elements such as mahat— and other things are not like this.
Because it does not pervade all things,
it is therefore different from nature (svabhāva).
Fifth, that which possesses a basis (savastuka):
When the great elements and other such entities are about to arise within birth and death,
they rely upon these thirteen components to enable the subtle body to revolve through birth and death, extending and contracting, and moving to and fro.
The intrinsic nature is not like this,
for it has no extension or contraction.
Sixth, "sinking" refers to:
When gross objects and other such things transform from their derivative forms back to their fundamental state, they can no longer be perceived;
this is called "disappearance" (*astaṅgama*).
For example, when the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) transform and dissolve into the five subtle potentials (*tanmātra*), the gross elements are no longer seen.
Even up to the point where the Great dissolves into its own nature,
even the Great cannot be seen;
the nature itself is not like this.
Because there is no turning or perishing. As for the seventh,
the "possessor of existence-parts" (bhavāṅga), it exists in all [beings], such as the Great Elements and so forth.
Because [conditioned things] consist of distinct parts,
their intrinsic nature is not like that;
it is eternal because it lacks distinct parts.
The eighth, the dependent nature,
refers to the great [ego] which depends on self-nature,
and the conceit of self (asmimāna) which depends on the great.
The five subtle elements (tanmātra) depend solely upon the ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra). The five gross elements and the other sixteen principles all depend upon the five subtle elements.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not like this,
because it does not arise dependent on another.
Ninth, that which belongs to another:
The great elements and so forth arise from their primary causes;
because the derivative products lack autonomy,
they are like [a son] while the father is still alive.
The child does not attain autonomy;
its intrinsic nature is not thus,
for it is without foundation because it exists for the sake of another.
Due to these nine kinds of causes,
the beginning and the end are entirely different;
therefore, they are said to be dissimilar.
The dissimilar has already been explained;
the similar shall now be explained.
Regarding that which is similar by nature:
He showed it by means of a verse:

The three virtues are inseparable; The object is equal, devoid of cognition, yet capable of producing both the root and the branch as if resembling [the subject]; I, conversely, am as if not resembling [it].
There are six kinds of similarity.
Regarding the first three qualities,
there are three qualities of transformation.
As for "transformations," these refer to the great ego (mahā-ahaṃkāra) up to the five gross elements (pañca-mahābhūta).
These twenty-three [principles] all possess the three qualities (guṇas).
First, pleasure;
second, suffering;
third, the darkness of delusion.
Since there are three virtues in the derivative,
we know that there are three virtues in the fundamental;
for the derivative does not depart from the fundamental.
For example, black cloth is produced from black threads;
the derivative and the source resemble one another.

Because these two are conjoined, the three *guṇas* appear as if they possessed consciousness.
It is, for example, like a heated vessel: it becomes hot through conjunction with fire and cold through conjunction with water.
In this way, these three qualities are associated with the knower; just as there is a knower who can form a determinate intention, it is therefore said that the non-knower is like the knower.
As for your statement that "a person is the agent" because this is a conventional expression following worldly usage:
I shall now answer this point:
because the three qualities (guṇas) are capable of acting,
they are like a creator who is impartial and straightforward.
Therefore, because of this conjunction, that which is not an agent is spoken of as being capable of acting.
It is like a certain Brahmin who mistakenly entered a band of thieves;
when the thieves killed or captured someone, he was likewise killed or captured along with them.
Because he accompanies the thief, he receives the name "thief";
the person and the self are likewise so,
as they accompany the agent.
According to worldly conventional usage,
I am said to be the agent.
The opponent says:
How can primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) come into union?
He answers in verse:
"I seek to see the three qualities; primordial nature remains solitary."
Just as the union of the lame and the blind gives rise to the world through their respective capacities,
so too do I seek to see the three qualities (guṇas); such is my intention.
I shall now perceive the self-nature (svabhāva) of the three qualities (guṇas);
therefore, I am conjoined with that self-nature.
That self-nature exists as something solitary; this is the cause of suffering, for only the person who possesses the capacity for knowledge and vision [perceives it].
Now, for the sake of enabling that [self] to exist independently,
its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) unites with the self; for this reason,
it is like a king uniting with his subjects.
"I should employ this person;
this person will also be in harmony with the king,
and the king should grant me the means of livelihood."
Because this king is harmonious through the principle of integration, he achieves his own self-nature; the principle of integration is likewise so.
This is because the self exists for the sake of perception, while self-nature exists as that which is other and solitary.
It is like the union of a cripple and a blind man.
Regarding this, there is an analogy: once, a caravan of merchants was traveling toward Ujjayinī when they were plundered by bandits and scattered in all directions.
There was one man born blind and another born lame whom the crowd had cast aside;
the blind man wandered aimlessly while the lame man sat watching.
The lame man asked:
"Who are you? The blind man replied, "I am one born blind;
because I do not know the way, I have been wandering aimlessly."
"Who are you? The cripple replied,
"I am a person born with a disability who can only see the path but cannot walk."
"Therefore, you should now place me upon your shoulder;
I can lead the way,
and you may carry me as we go."
Thus these two people, having come together in harmony, eventually arrive at their destination;
this harmony is accomplished through purposeful intent.
Upon reaching the destination, they each depart from one another.
In this way, when one perceives the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the "I," one immediately attains liberation.
This self-nature also causes the "I" to exist alone, such that all individual characteristics are abandoned.
As for the arising of the world from meaning, it is because people perceive the self-nature of others as existing independently.
By virtue of these two meanings, conjunction is achieved.
This conjunction is capable of producing the world;
it is, for example, like men and women who, through the union of both, are able to procreate a child.
In this way, the Self, conjoined with primordial nature (prakṛti),
is able to produce the Great One (mahat) and the other principles.
The opponent says:
It has already been explained that the world arises through the power of conjunction.
What is the sequence of this arising?
To answer by means of a verse:
The self-nature arises in succession; within the sixteen [evolutes] of the great *ahaṃkāra*, there are five. From this, the five great elements arise.
Regarding "the self-nature arises in succession": [it means as follows].
Self-nature is sometimes called the Supreme Cause,
and sometimes called Brahmā.
It is also called "Upholding the Multitude.
If it were to arise sequentially,
then because its intrinsic nature would be inherently existent, there would be nothing from which it could arise.
The self-nature is primordially great.
This greatness is sometimes called awakening (bodhi) and sometimes called perception (saṃjñā).
It is sometimes called "pervasive," sometimes called "knowledge," and sometimes called "wisdom."
Because this "Great" (mahat) consists of wisdom, it receives the name "wisdom.
From the Great arises the conceit of "I-am-ness" (asmimāna).
This conceit of "I-am-ness" is also called the first of the five great elements.
Some are called "transformation" (pariṇāma) and some are called "blazing" (jvalana).
From pride (māna), sixteen [types] arise in succession.
The sixteenth [category] consists of the five subtle elements (tanmātra).
As for the five subtle elements:
First, sound; second, touch; third, color; fourth, taste; fifth, fragrance.
These fragrant objects consist solely of substance and capacity.
Next are the five cognitive faculties.
The five faculties of cognition are:
first, the ear; second, the skin; third, the eye; fourth, the tongue; and fifth, the nose.
Next are the five faculties of action.
The five faculties of action are:
first, the tongue; second, the hands; third, the feet; fourth, the male and female organs; and fifth, the organ of excretion.
Next is the mental faculty.
These sixteen arise from the conceit of "I am";
therefore, they are called the sixteen great conceits (*mahāmāna*).
Furthermore, within these sixteen, there are five.
From this, the five great elements arise.
There are five [aspects] of the sixteen;
only the five [subtle elements] give rise to the five great elements.
Sound arises solely from the great element of space;
touch arises solely from the great element of wind;
and form arises solely from the great element of fire.
Taste arises solely from the water element;
fragrance arises solely from the earth element.
By perceiving the transformation of these three dharmas—their own nature and their variations—one attains liberation from the self.
I have now finished my exposition.
The opponent says:
"You have already explained that the Great [Element] arises from primordial nature (svabhāva)."
What are the characteristics of the "Great"?
Answering in verse:
Decisive wisdom is called "Great"; It is the wisdom of the Dharma, free from desire.
The characteristic of the sovereign being (īśvarasattva) is the opposite of this;
it is the decisive knowledge (*niścayajñāna*) that is called "great.
What is meant by "decisive knowledge"?
That is to say, when one perceives that "this object is named X" and "this person is named Y," such cognition is called definitive knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*).
This definitive knowledge is precisely what is termed "great."
This great [state] has eight parts:
four parts are called joy,
and four parts are called darkness and delusion.
Regarding the "sharing of joy":
it refers to the Dharma, wisdom, freedom from desire, and mastery.
What are the characteristics of the Dharma?
Yama-ni-yama. There are five aspects of Yama:
first, the absence of anger.
Second, revering one's teacher;
third, internal and external purity;
fourth, reducing one's food and drink.
Fifth is non-negligence.
Niyama also consists of five:
first, abstaining from killing.
Second, refraining from stealing;
third, truthful speech;
fourth, celibacy.
It is free from the five kinds of flattery and crookedness,
and is accomplished through ten aspects;
for this reason, it is called the Dharma.
What is called wisdom?
Wisdom is of two kinds:
first, external wisdom.
The second is internal knowledge;
external knowledge consists of the six Vedāṅgas.
First, the treatise on etymology (śabdavidyā);
second, the treatise on logic (hetuvidyā);
third, the treatise on cosmology (adhyātmavidyā).
Fourth, the *Cūḍapanthaka-śāstra* and its commentary;
fifth, the *Chandoga-śāstra*;
sixth, the *Nirukta-śāstra*.
The knowledge of these six bases is called external.
Internal knowledge refers to the three qualities (guṇas) and the self (ātman).
The wisdom between these two is attained through external wisdom;
the world is attained through internal wisdom; and liberation [is attained] through both.
What is detachment from desire?
There are two kinds of detachment from desire:
first, external; second, internal.
Regarding external things, one has already perceived the suffering and distress of the three times:
namely, the time of seeking them, the time of guarding them, and the time of losing them.
Furthermore, one perceives two kinds of faults in mutual attachment and killing;
because of this perception, one leaves home out of desire for renunciation.
Yet, though thus free from desire, one has not yet attained liberation.
This cause for detachment from desire is accomplished through external knowledge.
As for internal detachment from desire,
it arises because one has already recognized that the person (puruṣa) is distinct from the three guṇas, and thus seeks to renounce the household life.
First one attains internal wisdom, and subsequently attains freedom from desire.
Because of this freedom from desire, one attains liberation;
yet because of external freedom from desire alone, one still remains within birth and death.
Because one is internally free from desire, one is able to attain liberation.
Regarding mastery (*vaśitā*),
there are eight kinds of mastery.
First, the subtlest is the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*);
second, the most light and wondrous is the mind;
third, the most pervasive is space.
Fourth, he attains whatever he intends to attain.
Fifth, he is the sovereign lord of the three worlds,
for he excels others in every respect.
Sixth, one can employ the objects of desire simultaneously according to one's wishes;
seventh, one is not dependent on others and is able to direct the beings of the three worlds to serve oneself.
Eighth is dwelling according to one's will,
which means dwelling at any time, in any place, and with any state of mind.
These four dharmas are the characteristics of a sattva.
If the sattva increases,
one is able to subdue rajas and tamas; at that time,
because of my great joy and delight, I obtain the four virtues beginning with the Dharma.
This is called the characteristic of *sattva*.
The opposite of this is *tamas*, which is the opposite of the four characteristics beginning with *dharma*.
First, unrighteousness;
second, lack of wisdom;
third, craving.
Fourth is lack of mastery.
These four factors are the characteristics of *tamas*.
Thus, if these four types of joy and four types of delusion are associated with *mahat*, [they constitute the faculty of pleasure].
In its extensive version, it consists of eight sections;
the time of transformation is that which was previously produced.
According to the Kaiyuan lu, the *Saptati-tantra* (Seventy Verses on Gold), Volume One, is also titled the *Saṃgha-śāstra*.
Alternatively, it is said in two fascicles:
"The above treatise was composed by the non-Buddhist seer Kapila;
it elucidates the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*)."
What is called Sāṃkhya refers to the *Kāpila-śāstra* mentioned in the sūtras.
Furthermore, in the two catalogs of the Inner Canon by Sengyou and Fei Changfang,
among the translations by Paramārtha, there are two fascicles of the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (The Seventy Verses on Gold) and additionally three fascicles of the *Saṃgha-śāstra*.
It is an error to claim that both [the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*] and the [present] treatise exist together. This treatise, as well as the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*,
are not the Buddha-dharma.
Now, among the various non-Buddhist schools,
these two treatises are considered superior due to their numerical excellence;
they were intended for those who, being widely learned, would refute the heterodox and manifest the correct.
First, one must thoroughly understand the tenets of heterodox paths;
therefore, I have translated this [text],
fearing that its meaning might otherwise be lost.
This was transmitted and thus included in the Canon.
*The Seventy Stanzas on Gold*, Middle Fascicle,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen Dynasty.
The outsider said: "The explanation of the 'Great' [self] is finished. What are the characteristics of pride (*māna*)? He answered in verse:
"Pride consists of the grasping at 'I' and 'mine. From this arise two kinds:
those born from eleven faculties, and those born from five, which are exclusively the five great elements."
Regarding "the conceit of 'I' and the grasping of 'mine':
what are the characteristics of the conceit of 'I'?
They are: 'my voice,' 'my touch,' 'my form,' 'my taste,' 'my fragrance,' and 'my merit that is desirable.'"
This "I" which I grasp is called the conceit of "I am.
Regarding the phrase "from this two kinds arise":
from this conceit of "I am," two types of transformations arise.
What are the two kinds?
First, those produced from eleven faculties;
second, those consisting solely of the five great elements.
The eleven faculties and the five objects have already had their names stated above;
the characteristic of the conceit "I am" has also been explained.
There are three kinds of *asmimāna*.
Which dharma arises following each one?
He answers in verse:
The eleven types of *sattva* arise from the transformation of the *ahaṃkāra*.
From the Great [Ahaṃkāra] arises the first-born Darkness (*tamas*), which alone is intensely blazing; from this, two kinds [of *sattva*] arise.
Regarding "the eleven types of *sattva* arise from the transformation of the *ahaṃkāra*": [text continues].
If joy increases within the awakening,
then conceit arises;
it can suppress both sorrow and delusion.
This conceit of "I" is the seed of delight;
the Noble Ones call it "transformation.
This is the conceit of transformation.
It can produce eleven faculties.
How is this known? It is because of the abundance of pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*saumanasya*).
Because it is luminous and pure, and because it can grasp its own objects,
these eleven are called the *sattva* family.
That which is born first from the Great [Prakṛti] is solely darkness (*tamas*).
If great darkness increases within,
then the conceit "I am" arises,
which is able to suppress both joy and sorrow.
Because this conceit of self (asmimāna) is the seed of delusion,
the Noble Ones call it the "Great Primordial" (mahāmūla).
This conceit of self gives rise to the five subtle elements (tanmātra).
The five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) are entirely of the nature of darkness and delusion;
they give rise to two kinds [of beings] through their blazing intensity.
If great suffering increases within,
then the conceit "I am" arises;
it can suppress pervasive joy and darkness.
Because this conceit of self (asmimāna) is the seed of sorrow,
the Noble Ones have designated it by the name "blazing fire.
This conceit of self gives rise to two kinds.
It can produce the eleven faculties and also produce the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth;
this is the transformation of the *sattva* element.
The conceit of self (asmimāna) can give rise to the sense-faculties;
it takes the blazing conceit of self as its companion. Why is this so?
That which is blazing undergoes transformation due to having an object;
that which is of the nature of *sattva* undergoes transformation due to lacking an object.
If the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) arises, it consists of eleven faculties.
It must take the blazing *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) as its companion;
this is the primary *ahaṃkāra*.
From it arise the five *tanmātras*, the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*), and so forth.
One must necessarily take the blazing conceit as one's companion.
Why is this so? Because there is no activity apart from darkness, delusion, and conceit.
Because there is the occurrence of blazing,
such blazing conceit (*asmimāna*) is able to produce eleven faculties (*indriya*).
It also gives rise to the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and so forth;
therefore, it is said that the blazing [fire] produces two kinds.
The opponent says:
It has already been stated that eleven faculties arise from the category of sentient beings (*sattva*). What are these eleven faculties?
To answer this, a verse says:
The ear-skin, eye, tongue, and nose—these five are called the faculties of cognition (*vijñāna-indriya*).
The tongue, hand, foot, male organ, and female organ—these five are called the faculties of action (*karma-indriya*).
Regarding "the ear-skin, eye, tongue, and nose—these five are called the faculties of cognition": [this refers to the five sensory organs].
Why are they called faculties (*indriya*)?
Because these five are able to apprehend sound, form, and so forth, they are called the faculties of cognition (*vijñānendriya*).
The tongue, hands, feet, male faculty, and the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are the five faculties of action (*karmendriya*).
What is meant by "acting as a root"?
It refers to speech and other such activities,
because these five function as causal agents (*kāraṇa*).
Therefore, the sages of old established the name "five faculties of action.
An opponent asks:
what are the functions of these ten faculties?
The auditory faculty arises solely from sound;
since it belongs to the same category as space,
it perceives only sound.
The tactile faculty arises solely from contact;
since it is of the same category as wind,
it perceives only contact.
The eye faculty arises solely from visible form;
it is of the same category as fire.
Therefore, it perceives only visible form.
The tongue-faculty arises solely from taste and is of the same category as water;
therefore, it perceives only taste.
The olfactory faculty arises solely from fragrance;
it is of the same class as the earth element.
Therefore, it perceives only fragrance.
The five faculties of action have five functions.
This faculty of the tongue is associated with the faculty of cognition;
it is capable of articulating names, phrases, and syllables.
The hand faculty is associated with the faculty of cognition;
it is capable of performing crafts, grasping, and so forth.
The foot faculty is associated with the faculty of cognition.
One who can travel paths both level and uneven possesses faculties that correspond to the faculty of human nature and the faculty of knowledge;
such a person is capable of engaging in play and delight, and of procreating children.
The faculty of great renunciation is associated with the faculty of knowledge;
it is able to cast away filth and impurities.
For this reason, they are called the ten faculties.
The outsider asked:
"What is the root of the mind?
He replied with a verse:
That which is capable of discrimination is the mind (*citta*). Regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*), it is said there are two kinds.
Because the three qualities (*guṇa*) undergo transformation and because they are distinct from the external [objects], each is different.

Regarding "that which is capable of discrimination is the mind; regarding the sense faculties, it is said there are two kinds": [this means that] the mind is that which discriminates, while the sense faculties are of two types.
The essence of the mind-faculty consists of two kinds of discrimination.
Why is this so? Because if this mind-faculty is associated with the faculty of knowledge (jñānendriya), [it is of one kind].
This is called the faculty of knowing;
if it is associated with the faculty of doing,
it is called the faculty of doing.
Why is this? Because this faculty of mind is able to discern and know the functions of the faculties,
as well as to discern and perform the functions of the faculties.
For example, there may be one person who is either skilled in craftsmanship or capable of eloquent exposition.
The mind-faculty (*cittendriya*) is also like this. Why is this mind called a faculty?
Because it resembles the ten faculties.
The ten faculties arise from the transformation of the conceit of "I";
the mind-faculty is likewise,
performing the same function as these ten faculties.
The ten faculties perform their respective functions,
and the mind-faculty performs them in the same way;
therefore, they receive the name "faculties" (*indriya*).
The outsider asks:
"Since the objects of the various faculties are each distinct, are the mental faculties not also distinct?
He replies:
That which is capable of discernment is precisely that matter.
It is like a person who hears that there is wealth and food in a certain place.
He then forms this thought:
"I shall go there; I will surely obtain fine food and material offerings.
Such a discrimination is a distinct mental factor arising from the mind.
Because they arise together and function together, yet are distinguished from one another, they are termed "faculties" (*indriya*).
Therefore, the faculties are only eleven in number.
The opponent says:
As for which of these eleven faculties can perform this function,
if one asks how such a doubt arises,
it is because the noble ones hold differing views.
Some say it is created by a person or a self;
others say...
It is produced by the sovereign creator;
some say it is produced by a self-existent being.
Such attachments as these differ from one another.
For this reason, I have given rise to doubt:
among these faculties and objects, eleven kinds must certainly arise from consciousness.
How is this known? These eleven faculties are able to grasp eleven objects;
since the great *asmimāna* (ego-conceit) lacks cognition by its very nature, it should not possess such capacity.
As stated in the *Lokāyata* (Worldly Entrance) treatise—
here translated as *Shijie ru* (世入)—
it can produce the white color of a goose and the green color of a parrot.
The peacock is born with variegated colors; I too am born from this.
Therefore, I now have doubt: from what do these eleven arise?
He replied:
In this treatise, the self is not the agent;
Īśvara is also not the agent;
nor does there exist any distinct dharma called "existence."
Therefore, as you have stated, the eleven faculties are not produced.
The opponent asks:
"If that is so, what dharma is able to produce them?"
The answer is:
Because the three qualities (guṇas) undergo transformation, because they are external, and because they are distinct from one another,
the three qualities exist within the conceit of self (ahaṃkāra).
In accordance with my intention, they are transformed into eleven faculties. What is my intention?
It is that these eleven external objects are each distinct from one another.
If a single faculty were to arise, it would be unable to apprehend [all objects] universally;
therefore, eleven faculties arise in turn,
each apprehending its respective object.
Therefore, the eleven faculties differ from one another.
Furthermore, as for your claim that that which lacks cognition cannot produce many [effects],
this argument is not tenable.
Because ignorance possesses many capacities,
as will be explained in this treatise.
To nourish its calf, the ignorant cow produces milk.
In order to liberate [beings] from the self and the person, the roots of ignorance are thus established;
therefore, the three qualities (guṇas), being characterized by ignorance, can produce the eleven faculties.
The opponent says:
I have now understood that these eleven faculties arise from the conceit "I am.
These eleven faculties are established in distinct positions;
by whom were they so arranged?
The eyes are situated at the highest point and can see distant forms;
the ears are located on either side and can hear distant sounds;
the nose is situated in a single place and can perceive odors that reach it.
The tongue within the mouth can perceive flavors as they arrive;
the skin-faculty, whether internal or external, perceives all touches upon their arrival;
and the tongue within the mouth can express names, phrases, and meanings.
The hands are located on the left and right, capable of grasping;
the feet are in the lower part of the body, capable of walking below the navel;
the two organs reside in a concealed place.
To avoid being constantly seen by others,
one can cultivate the joy of renunciation;
for the faculty of mind has no fixed location.
It is capable of performing the function of discrimination.
As for who established these various faculties,
it was created by me, the Sovereign Creator.
Question: Is it produced by a distinct cause?
Answer: This treatise states: [as follows].
I am not the cause; Īśvara is also not the cause.
Only self-nature (svabhāva) is the true cause.
From the primal nature (prakṛti) arise the three qualities (guṇas) and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The ego-sense functions according to the will of the self;
by means of this, the three qualities establish the various faculties (indriyas).
Therefore, it is said that because the three qualities (guṇas) undergo transformation, differ externally, and are distinct from one another,
there are two intentions regarding the proximity or distance of the faculties (indriya):
first, for the purpose of avoidance.
The second is for the protection of the body;
it serves to avoid and distance oneself,
because one sees from afar and hears from afar, and thus rejects and abandons [the object] beforehand.
It is for the sake of protecting the body;
one only perceives them when the eight types of sensory objects reach the sense faculties,
because one desires to attend to the body so that it may flourish and increase.
The outsider asks:
"What function do these eleven faculties perform?
He answers in verse:
"Seeing only objects such as forms is the function of the five sense-faculties of cognition.

Regarding the phrase "seeing only objects such as forms is the function of the five sense-faculties of cognition": [it means that] seeing only objects such as forms constitutes the activity of the five faculties of sensation. "Speaking, grasping, walking, and playing are the functions of the five faculties of action. [This means that] speaking, grasping, walking, and playing constitute the activity of the five faculties of action.
The eye perceives only forms;
form is the objective domain of the eye.
It can only perceive and cannot discern or grasp.
The same applies to the other faculties.
Each functions solely by illuminating its own respective object.
The faculty of cognition (jñānendriya) is able to illuminate the object, while the faculty of grasping (ādānendriya) performs the function of apprehending it.
The function of the faculty of cognition has already been explained.
Next, the function of the faculty of action is explained:
speech is the objective sphere of the tongue-faculty.
Holding this is the sphere of the hands;
walking is the sphere of the feet;
playing for pleasure and procreating are [the spheres of] the genitals.
They serve as the bases and objects for the faculties;
having abandoned them, they are the objects of great loss.
The function of the faculties has thus been explained.
Next, the objects of the state of great *asmimāna* (I-conceit) shall be explained. 1.
The three [objects] characterized by their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*). 2. The thirteen uncommon objects. 3.
The objects common to the sense faculties (*indriya*). 4. The five winds, such as *pāna* and so forth.
The great matter of conceiving "I" is the characteristic of pride;
this characteristic is itself the object of pride.
Its conceptual differentiation constitutes the characteristic of the mind.
This characteristic is precisely the mind-object.
Regarding the thirteen uncommon objects:
because each of the ten faculties has its own respective object, and because the characteristics of the great conceited mind each perform their own respective functions.
Therefore, it is said that their functions are distinct.
Regarding the five winds, such as *pāna* and so forth, which share common functions among the various faculties:
if one speaks of the meaning of non-common functions, it follows by implication that there must also be common functions.
As for "not sharing activities," it is like each person having their own wife. As for "sharing activities," [it is when they have one wife in common].
It is like many people sharing a single servant;
who among them employs her?
It is the five kinds of winds.
First is *praśvāsa* (exhalation);
second is *āśvāsa* (inhalation);
third is *udāna* (upward-moving breath).
The fourth is vāna; the fifth is vāmana.
These are the five winds.
All the faculties share a single function.
As for the *pāna* wind,
the mouth and nose are its pathways.
Apprehending external objects is its function;
that is to say, "I am" and "I act"—
this is its active operation.
The opponent asks:
"By which faculty is this *pāna* produced?
The answer is:
These thirteen faculties function as a single entity,
just like a bird in a cage:
when the bird moves, the cage moves.
The same applies to the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Because they are moved by the *pavana* wind,
all thirteen faculties are set in motion.
Therefore, these thirteen faculties share the same function.
As for the *apāna* wind,
upon seeing anything fearsome, it immediately contracts and withdraws from it.
If this wind is excessive,
it causes a person to become timid and weak. As for the udāna wind:
"I wish to ascend the mountain.
I am superior; others are not as capable. I am able to do this."
If this wind is excessive,
it causes one to become self-exalting,
thinking "I am superior," "I am wealthy," and so forth.
This is the matter of the udāna;
as for the vāyana wind,
it pervades the entire body.
It is also utterly detached from the body.
If this wind is excessive,
it causes a person to become estranged from others and unable to find peace and happiness.
If this wind gradually withdraws,
part by part, until it has completely departed as if in death,
it then ceases; such is the Vāmana wind.
It resides in the heart region;
its function is to sustain and maintain [the body].
If this wind is excessive, [it causes]...
Causing one to be stingy and to seek wealth and companions—
these are the five matters of wind,
all produced by the thirteen faculties.
The thirteen faculties that are unique and their respective functions have already been explained.
Now, the simultaneous arising and the sequential arising [of these faculties] shall be explained.
It is stated in verse:
The arising of conceit, the faculties, or both, sequentially;
having seen or not yet seen the object; the three arisings first depend on the faculties.
Regarding "the arising of conceit, the faculties, or both, sequentially": [this refers to] the sequence of their occurrence.
If one perceives a form, the great conceit (*māna*), the mental faculty (*manas*), and the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) arise simultaneously to grasp a single object.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the other faculties;
four [mental factors] arise simultaneously.
Taking the same object together and arising in succession is like a person walking along a path.
Suddenly seeing a tall object, one immediately gives rise to doubt:
whether it is a person or a tree stump.
If one sees birds gathering [upon it], [the doubt is resolved].
Or seeing vines entwined around it,
or seeing deer nearby,
one immediately realizes it is a stump.
If one sees them shaking their robes,
or sees them stretching or contracting [their limbs],
one then realizes that they are human beings.
In this way, the roots of the conceited mind arise in succession.
Just as it is with what is seen by the eye,
one should know that the sequence for the ear and the other sense organs is likewise.
Regarding the threefold arising based first on the faculties with respect to objects already seen and not yet seen:
it has already been explained how the three types of dharmas already seen arise sequentially based on the faculties;
now, it shall be explained how the three types of dharmas not yet seen likewise arise sequentially based on the faculties.
As stated in the verse:
At the very end of the kalpa, there shall be such people who,
relying on wrong views and wrong conduct, will slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
First, they perversely transform their parents, friends, and kinsmen,
opening up the four paths to evil; they lead others into these [paths],
just as it was in the future and the past.
Based on the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), three phenomena arise in succession.
These three phenomena first arise based on the external faculty.
The opponent asks:
These thirteen instruments are devoid of cognition.
If they were not dependent upon persons and the faculty of sovereignty (*adhipati*),
how could each of them individually perceive its own respective object?
He replied with a verse:
Thirteen [factors] do not depend on another; They can perform their own functions.
In my view, these are the causal conditions; There is no other teaching that creates them.
Thirteenth, regarding the point that one does not perform one's own actions through another:
it has already been stated in this treatise that Īśvara and the self (*ātman*) are not the agents.
Therefore, the thirteen instruments of action function according to their own spheres and through their own capacity, not by means of another,
just as in the case of a brahmin practitioner of the holy life who was asked:
"In such-and-such a place there is a master of the Vedas who can teach his disciples so that they may learn as they wish."
"I shall now certainly go there to study.
This is precisely what constitutes such a realization;
having attained a sense of great self-importance through this conceit, one forms such a calculation.
I shall take away all the accoutrements belonging to the brahmins,
so that I may go there with an undistracted mind.
Having given rise to the conceit of "I" in this mind,
it makes this discrimination:
"Which Veda should I study first?"
"Are you studying the Sāmaveda?
Are you studying the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda?
Having thus discerned his external faculties and his mental discrimination, [the teacher asked].
The eyes can see the path;
the ears hear the words of others;
the hands hold the water pitcher.
Their feet are able to tread upon the road,
each performing their respective tasks.
It is like a leader of bandits who issues a command, saying:
"In coming and going, in advancing and halting, all must obey my commands.
The entire host of thieves has already complied with this order;
likewise, it is the same with the various sense faculties.
Awakening is like the leader of the bandits;
the other faculties are like the bandit hordes.
This is because one has already known the awakening-intention.
Each performs its own function.
The outsider says:
"These are the thirteen instruments of action."
Each grasps its respective object;
is this for oneself, or is it for another?
The answer is:
In my view, this is due to causes and conditions;
there is no separate teaching that creates it.
This meaning has already been explained previously.
Since the "self" (ātman) must perform actions,
the three guṇas produce the sense organs for the sake of manifesting and grasping objects for the self.
If you say that these sense-faculties are devoid of cognition, how can they act?
The answer is:
these sense-faculties do not come to depend upon this [body] as independent entities; rather, it is through the teaching within this [context] that they are made to act.
Only I am conjoined with my own nature;
thus I give rise to this thought:
"You should manifest yourself so that I may exist alone."
This is my intention. Therefore,
the three qualities (guṇas) are able to produce the various faculties,
each performing its respective function in accordance with my will.
Regarding the phrase "one who has departed from the notion of self," there is no other teaching.
The opponent says:
Among these twenty-four, how many names and meanings can function as instruments?
Answering in verse:

The instruments of action number thirteen; there are ten types of agents that can perform, draw forth, grasp, and illuminate their respective functions. The tongue 5. The body 6. The mind 7. Form 8. Sound 9. Odor 10. Taste 11. Tangible objects 12. Mental phenomena (dharmas) 13. Consciousness These thirteen constitute the instruments of action. Furthermore, there are ten types of agents capable of performing, drawing forth, grasping, and illuminating these functions: 1. The agent of seeing 2. The agent of hearing 3. The agent of smelling 4. The agent of tasting 5. The agent of touching 6. The agent of cognizing 7. The agent of form 8. The agent of sound 9. The agent of odor 10. The agent of taste 11. The agent of tangible objects 12. The agent of mental phenomena 13. The agent of consciousness Thus, the instruments of action number thirteen.
