In this treatise, it is stated in various places that the instruments of action are definitively only thirteen:
the five faculties of cognition, the five faculties of action, and the mind associated with discernment (*vitarka*) and conceit (*māna*).
What function do these thirteen perform?
They are capable of drawing forth, grasping, and illuminating;
their functions are of ten kinds.
The five sense objects, such as sound, and the five activities, such as speech—
these ten constitute the "objects.
These objects are of three kinds.
First, that which should be drawn; second, that which should be illuminated; third, that which should be grasped.
Among these, the three objects are what is drawn, while the five types of knowledge are what possess the illumination.
The five are the instruments of action and their maintenance;
based on these three matters, thirteen faculties are established.
Therefore, it is said that they should be drawn forth, maintained, and illuminated.
The opponent asks: How many faculties apprehend objects of the three periods of time?
How many apprehend objects of the present?
He answers in verse:
The internal faculties possess three [kinds of objects]; the ten external faculties possess three kinds of objects.
The external faculties grasp present objects; the internal faculties grasp objects of the three time periods.
Regarding "the internal faculties possess three": [this refers to the three types of objects].
The three types of conceit regarding awakening are called the internal instruments,
because they do not grasp external objects.
Therefore, it is established as "internal," because it is capable of accomplishing the skillful means of my intention;
for this reason, it is called "endowed."
Regarding "the ten external faculties possess three objects":
the ten external faculties consist of the five cognitive faculties and the five active faculties.
Because they are able to grasp external objects,
they are called "external requisites.
As for the three types of objects:
This is the root of the conceited mind;
the ten bases serve as its objects.
It is like a master employing subordinates.
In this same way, the three faculties can likewise cause the ten external bases to function;
as for the external bases, they apprehend present objects.
These ten faculties take present objects as their domains.
How is it known that they grasp [their objects]?
The ear faculty grasps only sounds of the present world.
Because it does not hear across two lifetimes.
This applies likewise to the ear faculty and even the nose faculty.
As for the tongue faculty, it is able to express present names, phrases, and syllables.
Regarding the future and the past, they cannot be so described.
As it is with the faculty of the tongue, so it is with the other four.
This refers to the internal apprehension of objects belonging to the three periods of time.
There are three types of conceit regarding cognition (*buddhi-māna*).
These are able to apprehend objects (*viṣaya*) of the three periods of time.
"Cognition" refers to that which can apprehend present objects such as jars and pots.
It can also apprehend the past,
such as when it apprehends King Mūrdhaja and others of former times;
it can also apprehend the future.
As it was said regarding the future, so it is with the destruction of the pride of all persons.
One reckons the objects of the three times as "mine," and the same applies to the mind and the faculties.
One discriminates the objects of the three periods of time because one seeks the future by recollecting the past; therefore,
it is said that one internally grasps the objects of the three periods of time.
The opponent asks:
How many faculties apprehend distinct objects,
and how many apprehend non-distinct objects?
He replied in verse:
Among the thirteen [faculties], the faculty of knowing (*jñānendriya*) perceives objects that are distinct or non-distinct;
the tongue has sound alone as its object; the remaining four all have the five types of sensory objects as their domain.
Regarding the thirteenth [category], the faculty of cognition (*jñānendriya*) that apprehends objects both with and without distinction:
among these thirteen faculties, five are faculties of cognition capable of apprehending objects that are either differentiated or undifferentiated.
As for the distinction,
it possesses the three qualities;
as for the lack of distinction, [it does not].
The single quality [of the heavens]:
just as there are five sensory objects in the heavens,
namely sound, touch, form, taste, and fragrance.
Because these five sense objects are undifferentiated and have the nature of uniform pleasure,
the five sense objects of the devas are free from sorrow and delusion;
whereas the five sense objects within the human realm possess differentiation.
Because it is constituted by association with pleasure, pain, and delusion,
the gods perceive objects through their sense faculties without discerning their distinctions;
humans, however, perceive objects through their sense faculties while being able to discern their distinctions.
That is to say, pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth are the objects [of the mind].
Therefore, it is known that the sense-faculties can apprehend objects that are either distinct or non-distinct.
As for the tongue, sound alone is its object.
The tongues of devas and the tongues of humans take only sound as their object;
they are able to express names, phrases, and meanings.
Regarding the remaining four [senses] and the five objects:
the substance of the hand faculty possesses the five objects and is capable of grasping the five objective spheres.
Just as the hand grasps a vessel,
so it is with the other sense organs. Thus,
these four organs, when established in relation to the five objects, all grasp the five objects.
Furthermore, the faculties have distinct characteristics.
As stated in verse:
Consciousness, together with its internal equipment, Is able to apprehend all objects.
Therefore, the three existences possess gates; all the faculties (*indriya*) are gates.
Consciousness (*buddhi*), together with the internal faculties, is able to grasp all objects (*viṣaya*).
This is because consciousness is constantly associated with the faculty of ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mind-faculty (*manas*).
It is said that awakening, together with its internal equipment,
is able to apprehend the objects of the three worlds and the objects of the three times; therefore,
it is said to be able to apprehend all objects.
Therefore, regarding the "three faculties as the doors":
these three faculties, beginning with discernment (*vitarka*),
are able to serve as the masters of all the gates.
If the three— perception and so forth— are present together in association with the eye faculty,
it is this eye faculty that can manifest and illuminate forms, whereas the other faculties cannot;
these three, gathered within a single faculty, are able to apprehend the objects of the three worlds as well as the three periods of time.
Therefore, these three are said to constitute the ten instruments (*karaṇa*).
As for the statement that "the remaining faculties are all doors," this means that the five faculties of cognition and the five faculties of action open and close in accordance with those three.
If the three [faculties] reside in the eye, the eye-gate is opened and can apprehend the external object;
the other gates are then closed and cannot cognize their respective objects.
Because they depend on others, they are merely gates and do not possess reality themselves.
Thus, these ten faculties are associated with the three groups and are able to apprehend all objects of the three worlds.
Furthermore, the verse says:

The various faculties are like lamps; according to their respective virtues, they mutually illuminate the dust of the three worlds. For my sake, I have returned them to the Awakened One. Regarding "the various faculties are like lamps":
[this means that] just as lamps shed light, so too do the faculties.
That is to say, the five knowledges, the five activities, the conceit of "I am," and the root of the mind are like a lamp placed in one location,
which illuminates all objects equally.
Thus, because these [qualities] are capable of illuminating the dust of the three worlds,
they are said to be like lamps.
Regarding their mutual differences according to their respective virtues:
They are mutually dissimilar:
the ear perceives sound but does not perceive form,
while the eye perceives form but does not perceive sound.
Even up to the nose, which perceives only odors and not tastes—
thus it is with the five cognitive faculties (*pañca-vijñānendriya*).
This is because the faculties are fixed in their correspondence with specific objects.
It is said that they are mutually distinct.
The same applies to their functioning as faculties (*indriya*).
The tongue, however, merely utters speech.
They cannot perform other functions;
even up to the point that *vitarka* (applied thought) performs only the function of decisive cognition,
while *māna* (pride) performs only the function of attachment.
The mind merely performs conceptualization;
therefore, it is said that they are mutually distinct.
What is the meaning of this distinction?
Following the three qualities (*guṇas*), the three qualities arise.
Because the arising of the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) differs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the various sense organs (*indriya*) all arise differently.
That which illuminates the objects of the three worlds as "I" is returned to the Awakened One (*buddha*).
These twelve faculties illuminate the dust of the world and are all returned to the Awakened One.
It is like when all the officials and citizens of a kingdom take the state's wealth and property and present it entirely to the sovereign.
In this way, because these various objects are handed over to cognition by means of the twelve faculties, cognition causes me to see them; therefore,
it is said that they are "handed over to my cognition."
The opponent asks:
"For what reason do the sense faculties not themselves illuminate the objects so that I may see them?
He answers in verse:

All my activities are accomplished through cognition; furthermore, they are seen later on. "All my activities are accomplished through cognition" means that [they are so accomplished] by means of cognition. "Furthermore, they are seen later on" refers to the fact that the self is subtle and distinct from them.
All my activities are accomplished through cognition. "Accomplished through cognition" means that they are so accomplished by means of cognition.
The functions of my activities differ across all realms—
whether in the human realm, the heavenly realm, or the animal realm—
ranging from the function of the ten subtle particles up to the eight kinds of sovereign powers.
The faculty of knowledge acts as the root.
The ten external faculties illuminate these objects and entrust them to awareness;
awareness receives them and hands them over to the person.
It enables people to obtain enjoyment;
through this sequence of awakening,
it can cause me to experience things as I wish.
One experiences the joy of mastery;
this continues until wisdom has arisen.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "later on one perceives the subtle difference from the self-natured self," "later on" refers to [the time after wisdom has arisen].
This means that when wisdom arises,
the self and intrinsic nature are distinct;
as for this distinction:
Because those who have not yet practiced the noble path cannot perceive it,
it is described as subtle.
This is the gateway among these distinctions.
Among these thirteen, it is only *buddhi* that causes the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
What is the characteristic of this "view"?

It is the view [of a self] as distinct from its own nature (*svabhāva*), distinct from the three *guṇas*, distinct from *buddhi*, distinct from *ahaṃkāra*, distinct from the eleven organs, distinct from the five *tanmātras*, distinct from the five gross elements, and distinct from the body.
Because such diverse perceptions have caused me to know [the truth],
I have attained liberation,
as previously explained.
If one knows that the twenty-five [principles] abide according to their respective places and paths—
whether with matted hair, a topknot, or a shaven head— and attains liberation equally through them,
therefore there is only a single awakening.
"This is my true instrument of proof.
The opponent says:
"The preceding verse has already explained that the various sense faculties are able to apprehend objects that are either differentiated or undifferentiated."
What is the distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation?
The verse answers:
"The five subtle elements (tanmātras) are without differentiation; from these arise the five gross elements (mahābhūtas)."
Regarding the statement that "the great elements have distinctions— namely, tranquility, fear, and delusion—
while the five [subtle] potentials (tanmātra) have no distinctions":
what do you mean by "distinction" and "non-distinction"?
Now I shall answer:
from the conceit of "I" arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*),
which are quiescent and characterized by joy and bliss.
This is indeed the dust of the devas;
there is no distinction between them,
for the devas are free from sorrow and delusion.
From these, the five great elements arise with their respective distinctions:
from sound, only space arises;

These five great elements have distinctions.
What are the characteristics of these distinctions?

Second, causing fear;
third, darkness and delusion.
These five great elements are the dust of man.
Why must the three characteristics of the great element of space necessarily be like a wealthy man entering a private inner chamber to enjoy the five sensory pleasures,

When there is no place of rest, darkness and delusion arise.
It is the same for the other great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Thus, these gods take the five subtle potentials (*tanmātra*) as their objects.
Because it is exclusively quiescent, there is no distinction.

The opponent says:
The distinctions between these have already been explained elsewhere.
Is there yet another distinction regarding this matter?
He replied:
Furthermore, there is another distinction,
as stated in the verse: "Subtle,
born of father and mother, and great— these are the three distinct differences."
Among the three [types of birth], the subtle and the permanent are distinct;
there are others characterized by retrogression and rebirth, and those born from parents. These three distinctions are:
all that pertains to the three worlds.
At first, a subtle body is produced,
consisting only of the five tanmātras;
this subtle body enters the womb at birth.
The union of the red and white elements increases the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*).
The mother’s six kinds of food and drink, through their flavors and moisture, nourish and increase the coarse body (*audārika-śarīra*).
Because these two paths of the mother’s food and drink are conjoined with the two locations [the subtle and coarse bodies], they obtain nourishment and benefit.
Just as the roots of a tree absorb water through its channels and thereby grow and flourish,
so too does the coarse body benefit from and increase through the nourishment of food and drink as they follow their respective pathways.
As is the measure of the subtle body,
so too is that of the coarse body.
The subtle body is called "internal."
The coarse body is called "external.
Within this subtle body, the dimensions and human characteristics of hands, feet, head, face, belly, and back are fully complete.
Among the four Vedas, there are sages who speak as follows:
The coarse body has six bases:
flesh, blood, and sinews—these three arise from the mother;
white hair and bone—these three arise from the father.
These six are the supporting bodies;
the external coarse body benefits the internal subtle body,
and this internal subtle body is sustained and benefited by the coarse body.
When about to emerge from the womb and once it has emerged,
the five external elements serve as its dwelling place; it is,
for example, like a prince for whom others construct a residence with various halls and pavilions.
This place should be inhabited, this place should be eaten, and this place should be slept in;
its intrinsic nature is likewise so.
It serves as the basis for both the subtle body and the coarse body, and is capable of generating the five great elements.
First is the great element of space,
which serves as the locus of non-obstruction.
Second is the great element of earth.
It is the locus for the manifestation of time.
The third life is the water element;
it is the locus of purity.
The fourth produces the fire element,
which serves as the locus for the digestion of food.
The fifth produces the wind element.
It can cause movement and dispersion.
Thus, there are three types of distinctions:
first, the subtle.
Second, birth from parents; third,
through mutual union— namely,
[the states of] tranquility, dreadfulness, darkness, delusion, and so forth.
These are the distinctions between the three names.
The opponent asks:
"Among these three distinctions, how many are eternal and how many are impermanent?"
The answer is:
Among the three, the subtle [mind] is eternally present;
the others have separate instances of retrogression and arising.
Among these three, five are manifested solely by the *vāsanās*.
Their subtle distinctions can give rise to the first body, which is permanent.
When the coarse body perishes and vanishes, [the former remains].
If a subtle body is associated with unrighteousness (adharma),
it undergoes the four modes of birth;
the first is birth as quadrupeds.
Second, those with wings;
third, those that move on their chests;
fourth, those with lateral forms.

second, as a deva; third, as a world-ruler (lokapāla); and fourth, as a human being.

this coarse body is produced by one's parents.
Some are devoured by birds, some are decomposed and ruined, and some are consumed by fire.

The opponent says:
"You have stated that when the bodies of one's parents pass away,

He answered in verse:
The body of a previous birth is without attachment; great pride and the five *tanmātras* revolve without grasping at objects.
That which possesses perfuming has subtle characteristics;
the body of a previous birth is without attachment.
In former times, that which is by nature transmigrates through birth in the world;
the subtle body is born first.

from intellect arises ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra);
from ego-consciousness arise the five subtle elements (tanmātras).

What are the characteristics of this subtle body?
It is like the form of a Brahmā deity, capable of receiving various sensory objects.
Because this body will later attain liberation.
As for being "unattached," it is as transmitted by the noble ones.
This subtle body may exist within the realms of animals, humans, or gods.
It cannot be obstructed by mountains, rocks, walls, or the like;
because it is subtle, it is also unchanging,
and as long as wisdom has not yet arisen, it is never separated from it.
This is what is called "permanence.
Regarding great pride and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*):
by how many factors is this body brought into existence?
Based on the seven kinds of subtle objects,
up to the sixteen kinds of coarse objects, what does this body do?
It revolves without grasping at objects;
this subtle body is associated with eleven faculties and exists within the four modes of birth.
It revolves through the three worlds;
it does not grasp objects,
nor is it associated with the eleven faculties.
If one were separated from the coarse body born of parents, there would be no power to grasp sensory objects.
As for that which possesses the subtle characteristics of perfuming,
this subtle body is of three kinds.
That which is perfumed by existence—
this "existence" will be explained later.
As for the three kinds of existence:
First, existence through the completion of wholesome karma;
second, existence through innate nature;
third, existence through transformation.
This subtle body, perfumed by these three [defilements],
possesses subtle characteristics because it is not perceived by noble ones (ārya).
This subtle body is capable of revolving through birth and death.
The opponent says:
"Since these thirteen faculties are sufficient for the cycle of birth and death, what need is there for a subtle body?
He answers in verse:
Just as a painting does not exist apart from a wall, and there is no shadow apart from a stump or the like;
if the body were apart from the five *tanmātras*, these thirteen [elements] would have no basis for abiding.
"Just as a painting does not exist apart from a wall, and there is no shadow apart from a stump or the like" means:
In this world, one observes that the two phenomena of the dependent and the basis are conjoined and inseparable,
just as painted colors depend upon a wall and have no separate existence apart from it.
Therefore, apart from the subtle body, these thirteen cannot abide.
Furthermore, apart from the trunk there is no basis for the shadow;
apart from fire, there is no light.
Apart from water, there is no cold;
apart from wind, there is no tangibility;
apart from space, the postures of movement cannot be established.
Thus, when separated from the subtle body,
these gross characteristics have no basis and cannot abide.

The outsider asked:
"What is the purpose of this subtle body in relation to the thirteen cycles of birth and death?
He replied with a verse:

The activity of the *ahaṃkāra* (I-maker) serves as the cause; because it depends on its cause and by virtue of that dependence, it is capable of manifesting all natures according to their own characteristics. As for the phrase "the activity of the *ahaṃkāra* serves as the cause":
it is like an actor who transforms through various changing appearances.
In my view, the intrinsic nature undergoes transformation because mental activity must be performed.
This mental activity is of two kinds:
first, that which begins with the experience of objects such as sound; [and second, that which begins with the experience of the self].
Second, regarding those who perceive people of the three virtues as being intermediate or final:
in the realm of Brahmā, the self and the person correspond to sounds and other sensory objects;
by causing them to enter into such correspondence, they shall subsequently be led to liberation.
The self-nature undergoes transformation to form the subtle body.
By what cause does this subtle body undergo transmigration?
It is due to causes and their dependence upon causes.
As for the causes, they refer to the eight kinds beginning with purity, which will be explained later.
Thus it is said in verse:
"By means of wholesome dharmas one ascends; By means of unrighteousness one descends."
Through the wisdom of causes, one attains weary detachment and liberation; conversely, this leads to bondage.
What further cause establishes these causes and their bases?
It is because of the all-pervasive power of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For example, just as a king within his own kingdom can act according to his will,
so too is intrinsic nature (svabhāva):
it is able to produce births as gods, humans, animals, and so forth.
It is said that they manifest different characteristics like a performer’s transformations;
for example, just as an actor may manifest the appearance of a deity, or the appearance of a king, or the appearance of a nāga, a ghost, or other such forms,
each being distinct from the others.
The subtle body is likewise;
it is associated with thirteen [mental factors].
Or, it enters the wombs of elephants, horses, and so forth.
They transform into the bodies of elephants, horses,
and so forth; or they enter the wombs of humans, devas, and so forth,
transforming into the bodies of humans and devas.
Therefore, it is said that according to its own nature, it is universally capable of transforming into various characteristics, like a skilled performer.
The opponent says:

To obtain these objects, one must perform various difficult tasks,
such as farming, raising livestock, serving a king, or engaging in trade.
If one is separated from these four matters, one might instead become a thief;
such pursuit of worldly objects is decidedly difficult to accomplish.
Because they afflict both themselves and others,
I see this matter and have sought to leave the household life;
such is the fifth person who possesses no liberation.
Because they lack true knowledge,
he further asks the second person:
"What dharma do you know that has enabled you to go forth?"
That person replied,
"I know that the five sensory objects can be obtained through seeking;
it is like the aforementioned expedient means of cultivating fields and so forth."
Having acquired the various sensory objects, it is difficult to guard them.
Why is this? Because the five aggregates are subject to contention.
Because one must oppress both oneself and others in order to guard these sensory objects,
and because I see that guarding them leads to suffering, I have left the household life to abandon such objects.
This sixth person, too, has no liberation.
Because they lacked true knowledge,
he next asked the third person:
"What do you know that you have been able to go forth?"
That person replied,
"I have already been able to cause those who have not yet attained [their goals] to attain them,
and to protect what has already been attained so that it is not lost."
These five sense objects naturally become lost through one's own enjoyment;
when they are lost, great suffering arises.
Seeing these faults in the loss of sense objects, one seeks to go forth from the household life.
This person likewise does not attain liberation because they lack true wisdom.
Next, he asks the fourth person:
"What do you know that you have been able to go forth?
The man replied, "I am already able to seek what has not yet been attained; having attained it, I am able to protect it."
Even after losing them, one is able to seek them again.
If that is so, why would one go forth?
For the five faculties are never satiated.
Because they seek excellence through successive stages,
and because I perceive the faults of these faculties, I have sought to leave the household life;
yet even this eighth person lacks liberation.
Because he lacked true knowledge,
he next asked the fifth man:
"What do you know that allows you to go forth?"
The person replied,
"I have already been able to seek out what was not yet obtained so as to obtain it;
having obtained it, I have guarded it so that it is not lost."
"Once used, it can be sought again;
if one seeks the most excellent, I am also able to obtain it.
If that is so, why have you gone forth?"
One should kill another for four reasons related to external objects;
if one does not kill them, the matter will not be accomplished.
For example, a farmer must cut the weeds and fell the trees.
When engaged in battle, one should kill people;
or when plundering another's wealth, one harms them;
or one speaks falsehoods with one's mouth, and so forth, including all manner of worldly transgressions.
Furthermore, because they perceive the fault that the self arises from sensory objects, they seek to leave the household life;
yet this ninth person likewise lacks liberation,
for due to their external aversion, they do not cultivate true wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that the first four rely on the internal and the latter five rely on the external; thus, they are combined into nine types of joy.
Regarding these nine kinds of joy, the Ṛṣis established nine names.
Because they can purify defilements and impurities, the nine types of joy are called "water":
first, moistening water;
second, shallow and deep water.
Third, Flowing Water;
fourth, Lake Water;
fifth, Skillfully Entering Water.
Sixth, the Water of Skillful Crossing;
seventh, the Water of Skillful Emergence;
eighth, the Water of Radiance.
The nine supreme purifying waters.
The opposites of these nine joys are called the nine incapacities (*navāśaktayaḥ*),
meaning they are not moistening, and so forth, up to not being supreme purifying waters.
The opponent says:
These three factors are contrary to establishment.
What dharma is called "establishment"?
He replied in verse:
“Through reflection, hearing, and recitation, one attains the three friends who are free from suffering.
By means of giving, one achieves the eight [perfections]; the first three constitute the hook of accomplishment.”
Regarding the eight factors accomplished through reflection, hearing, recitation, and even giving:
these eight types can be achieved through six practices.
For example, there was a certain Brahmin who left the household life to study the Path and reflected as follows:
"What is the most excellent? What is real? What is the final ultimate?
By what practice is wisdom attained and made manifest?
Having reflected thus, he immediately attained wisdom.

One gives rise to wisdom regarding the twenty-five principles of reality: that the primal nature (prakṛti) is distinct, consciousness (buddhi) is distinct, ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is distinct, the five subtle elements (tanmātra) are distinct, the eleven organs (indriya) are distinct, the five gross elements (mahābhūta) are distinct, and the true self (puruṣa) is distinct.
Based on this wisdom, six kinds of contemplation arise.
First, one contemplates the five faults of the great elements;
seeing these faults, one gives rise to weary detachment.
That is, one is detached from the five great elements;
this is called the stage of reflection.
Second, one contemplates the faults of the eleven faculties.
Seeing the faults [of cyclic existence], one gives rise to revulsion and immediately abandons the eleven faculties;
this is called the stage of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*).
Third, using this wisdom to contemplate the defects of the five subtle elements (tanmātras),
one perceives those defects and gives rise to revulsion; thus,
one immediately becomes detached from the five subtle elements.
This is called "entering the stage of suchness.
Fourth, by contemplating the faults of pride and the eight errors of the view of mastery, one gives rise to revulsion and thereby abandons pride and the like.
This is called reaching the state [of the path].
Fifth, observing the faults through contemplation;
seeing these faults gives rise to revulsion.
One immediately attains the stage called "Withdrawal" (saṃkoca), which is free from discursive thought;
one contemplates the faults of intrinsic nature and,
seeing these faults, develops weary detachment.
This is the very absence of intrinsic nature.
This state is called "solitary existence.
Because this Brahmin contemplated in this manner, he attained liberation.
This [attainment] is called "accomplished through reflection" because it is achieved by means of reflection;
the accomplishment through reflection has already been explained.
Next, the meaning of accomplishment through hearing is explained.
For example, a certain brāhmaṇa, upon hearing the sound of another reciting,
thought that the self-nature was distinct from cognition, and so on, up to the true self being distinct; yet it was merely by hearing this sound of recitation [that he conceived such distinctions].
Having already awakened to and known the twenty-five principles,
one enters the stage of contemplation (*cintā-avasthā*): by departing from the five great elements (*mahābhūta*),
one enters the stage of capacity (*śakti-avasthā*), and by departing from the eleven faculties (*indriya*).
Entering the stage of *yathābhūmi*, one is free from the five *tanmātras*;
entering the stage of *prāpti*, one is free from pride and the like;
entering the stage of *saṃkoca*, one is free from *buddhi*.
Entering the state of solitary existence and being free from intrinsic nature is called liberation.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning established through hearing.
Next, the meaning of recitation and study is explained.
It is accomplished through eight divisions of wisdom.
For example, there was a brahmin who went to the house of a teacher.
First, the desire to hear;
second, listening with focused attention;
third, receiving and retaining.
Fourth, retention;
fifth, knowing the meaning of the phrases;
sixth, reflection.
Seventh is discernment;
eighth is causing entry into reality as it is.
These are called the eight divisions of knowledge.
Through this wisdom, one attains twenty-five meanings.
Regarding the third point—entering the six practices to attain liberation and depart from suffering—there are three aspects:
first, departing from internal suffering.
For example, a certain brahmin, oppressed by internal suffering such as a headache,
went to a physician; once his illness was cured,
he developed a desire to understand the origin of that internal suffering.
Desiring to know how to extinguish the cause of this suffering,
one approaches a teacher’s household and gives rise to the eight stages of knowledge (*aṣṭajñānabhāga*).
By attaining the twenty-five meanings and entering the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍākārābhigama*), one achieves liberation.
This is established by internal suffering; as with bodily suffering, so too is mental suffering.
Second, there is the removal of external suffering, as in the case of a certain brāhmaṇa who was oppressed by external suffering.
This refers to being unable to endure the afflictions caused by humans, animals, birds, or even wood and stone;
thus, one gives rise to the desire to know the cause for the cessation of suffering and goes to the teacher’s residence to cultivate the eight branches of knowledge.
One attains liberation by realizing the twenty-five meanings through the contemplation of the six modes of conduct.
This accomplishment is achieved through external suffering and the third [type] relies upon celestial suffering.
For example, there was a certain brahmin who was oppressed by celestial sufferings—
namely, cold, heat, rain, and so forth—
which he was unable to endure.
One approaches a teacher to seek the eightfold wisdom.
By attaining the twenty-five meanings and entering the contemplation of the six practices, one achieves liberation.
This is the attainment of the seven kinds of spiritual friends.
It is not attained through the division of the eight knowledges;
rather, wisdom is obtained from virtuous friends.
Upon reaching the culmination of wisdom, one attains liberation.
Regarding those who become [monastics] due to eight causes:
for example, there was a certain brāhmaṇa who was loathed by others;
knowing that others detested him, he therefore left the household life.
Having already left the household life, his teacher and fellow practitioners also felt aversion toward him and did not grant him wisdom;
realizing his own meager merit, he went to live in a remote village.
Thinking that there were no brahmins in this place where he might dwell,
he went to reside there and received much alms-food;
what remained, he gave back to his friends and relatives.
Even down to the women and the herdsmen,
all the villagers came to love and cherish him.
When the summer retreat was about to end,
All the people together offered him alms, including three staffs, a water pitcher, and various garments.
Approaching the assembly of Śakra,
he spoke to the people at that time, saying:
"Who among you can return with me to our native great kingdom to behold this assembly?
If any wish to go, let each person take goods for me to carry there.
Once we have arrived at the teacher's house in that place..."
He selects the finest items to offer to his teacher,
while the remaining items are distributed in order to his fellow students;
thus, both his teachers and friends develop feelings of affection for him.
The Teacher immediately bestows upon them wisdom;
through this wisdom, they reach ultimate knowledge and thereby attain liberation.
This is accomplished by means of giving.
Regarding these eight accomplishments,
the sages of old established another set of names:
first, self-accomplishment.
Second, accomplishment through skillful deliverance;
third, accomplishment through complete deliverance;
fourth, accomplishment through joyful deliverance.
The fifth is accomplished through the perfection of joy;
the sixth is accomplished through the perfection of supreme joy;
the seventh is the accomplishment of love.
When these eight are fully accomplished through pervasive love, they are called the "eight masteries. If these eight are reversed,
they are called the "eight incapacities."
This refers to the inability to cross over,
up to the inability to love universally;
thus, these eleven faculties fall into the category of incapacity.
Furthermore, the seventeen knowledges (*jñāna*) that are incapable of harming become twenty-eight [incapacities].
These doubts that are incapable [of harm] joyfully transform into fifty meanings; this has already been explained.
Regarding the first three accomplishments of the hook:
it is like a drunken elephant that, once subdued by a hook, can no longer act according to its own will or exercise its freedom.
These five doubts and twenty-eight incapacities [are likewise brought under control].
The nine types of joy are suppressed [by this].
The world does not attain true knowledge;
for if one is separated from true knowledge, the eightfold path cannot exist.
It is said that the first three are the hooks of accomplishment.
Next, having abandoned doubt and being incapable of [further] hesitation, one joyfully applies diligent effort to accomplish the eight kinds.
An opponent says:
It has already been stated previously that it is because of the essential characteristics of all that is perfumed (*vāsanā*) that one revolves in birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
These essential characteristics are of two kinds.
First, the subtle body and its characteristics exist at the moment of initial birth;
second, there is the physical body produced by the parents and the eleven sense organs.
The eight [consciousnesses] associated with one another are subject to perfuming, and thus they revolve in birth and death.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
which arises first?
With the essential nature and characteristics as the priority,
and with all conditioned phenomena as the priority, he replied in verse:
Apart from existence, there is no distinct characteristic;
apart from subtle characteristics, there is neither the name "characteristic" nor the name "existence. Therefore, arising is of two kinds.
Regarding "apart from existence, there is no distinct characteristic": [text continues].
If one is separated from all existents, their essential nature cannot be established;
for example, fire cannot be established if it is separated from heat.
If there were no subtle characteristics, nothing would exist.
If one were separated from subtle characteristics, all existence would not be established;
it is just as heat cannot be established apart from fire.
These two phenomena are mutually dependent, like fire and heat.
"These phenomena arise together like the two horns of an ox;
because both characteristic and name exist, there are two kinds of arising.
This means that there are two names for the transformation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
First is the arising of characteristics and names;
second is the arising of existence.
At the initial birth within the cycle of birth and death, both types are simultaneously present.
The opponent says:
This arising has only two kinds;
there is no other name for it.
The answer is:
Among those sages of old who established distinct names, first is "the one who liberates oneself.
This person is most keenly focused on self-reflection, thereby attaining *prajñā* and achieving liberation.
Because it does not rely on the instruction of another, it is said that "one achieves self-deliverance.
One attains it through one's own contemplation because it does not depend on others;
thus, it is *prajñā*.
If the waves can escape this [shore] and reach that [shore],
it is therefore called "crossing over"; at the time of reaching it,
it is termed "liberation."
Liberation is what is called "accomplishment.
The cause is termed "crossing over" (tú) and the fruit is termed "accomplishment" (chéng).
This crossing over and accomplishment are attained through one's own reflection; therefore, it is said that one "crosses over and accomplishes for oneself" (zì dù chéng).
The meaning of the subsequent seven instances of accomplishment is no different;
it is merely that their distinct names vary.
Second, as for accomplishment through skillful means:
Because they rely on others, they attain the perfection of *prajñā* and liberation.
These individuals possess weak and inferior faculties; relying on the instruction of others, they achieve much for their own benefit and are able to attain deliverance.
Therefore, it is called "successful completion through skillful means.
Regarding the third type, "complete successful completion," this is attained solely through the instruction of another.
Therefore, they are called "complete.
Furthermore, their spiritual faculties are inferior.
Regarding those who attain completion through the faculty of joy:
This person, oppressed by internal suffering—
namely, headaches and the like—
goes to a teacher to seek treatment.
To obtain a temporary release from internal suffering is the first joy;
yet one reflects that this release is not a permanent one.
Knowing that when one exists alone, one is eternally liberated, he went to a teacher of Sāṃkhya to study Prajñā, seeking to achieve liberation; upon attaining it, he experienced joy once more.
From these two joys, his name was derived.
This is called "Accomplishment through the Joyful Deliverance.
Regarding the fivefold accomplishment through the joyful deliverance:
this person is oppressed by both internal and external suffering.
One goes to the teacher and requests that the two sufferings be treated.
Once the two sufferings have temporarily ceased,
this constitutes the two joys.
Knowing that this was not permanent liberation,
he sought out a teacher to study and achieve deliverance;
having attained it, he received the name "Joyfully Receiving" (Huanxi Shou) due to his profound joy.
Regarding the sixth, "fulfilling joy":
this person is fully oppressed by the three types of suffering.
The first is internal suffering.
Headaches and the like;
second, external suffering,
such as swords and staves.
The suffering of the three calamities—
wind, rain, cold, heat, and so forth—
led them to seek out their teacher and request his treatment.
Once the treatment had cured him,
he was named Bianxi (Universal Joy);
yet he knew that this was not permanent liberation.
Because he attained liberation through training under his teacher,
he was named accordingly;
thus, he was called Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Regarding "one who has attained perfection through the teacher’s affection": it refers to one whom the teacher, out of compassionate love, instructs until they attain perfection;
it is from the teacher that this name is received.
Regarding the eighth, "success through universal love":
although this person is hated by all,
they obtain wealth and practice giving.
Consequently, one becomes beloved by all;
everyone desires that such a person attain liberation.
Therefore, it is said that "universal love leads to the accomplishment of deliverance."
There are eleven types of incapacity resulting from the impairment of the faculties;
seventeen types of incapacity resulting from the destruction by knowledge.
Together, these constitute twenty-eight types of incapacity.
The fifty [categories] consisting of five doubts, nine joys, and eight accomplishments have already been explained.
Regarding the first three accomplishments, as for the hook (āṅkuśa):
there are five doubts, twenty-eight that cannot be surpassed, and nine joys.
These eight joys are the hooks for accomplishing the household.
Although one ought to attain the eightfold liberation, one does not obtain it because of three [obstacles].
Just as a rutting elephant should be self-governing but cannot exercise its will due to the hook, so too [the practitioner] lacks mastery.
The eight attainments (*aṣṭa-samāpatti*) are likewise.
One necessarily attains the eight attainments by means of true knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*);
however, because one is hooked by the three [fetters], one does not attain true knowledge.
One must abandon the first three and diligently cultivate the latter eight.
The opponent says:
Next, [the text] poses a question by restating the preceding meaning.
Regarding the subsequent inquiry into priority and sequence:
as for the fact that all things which possess the essence and characteristics of habitual perfuming revolve in birth and death,
this has already been explained above.
All existences are the eight existences;
that is to say, four dharmas and four non-dharmas.
As for the four dharmas:
First is the Dharma, second is wisdom, third is freedom from desire, and fourth is mastery.
To reverse these four dharmas constitutes the four non-dharmas.
The eighth is called "existence" (bhava).
The perfuming by the first four dharmas enables one to attain the heavenly realms;
the perfuming by the latter four non-dharmas does not.
It is capable of causing one to obtain either the path of humans or the path of animals.
That which is perfumed is the essence-characteristic (tǐxiàng).
There are two kinds of essence-characteristics.
The subtle body (sūkṣma-deha) consists of the five tanmātras, which are the objects of the conceit of self-nature (svabhāva-ahaṃkāra).
That which arises from the five tanmātras and is associated with the eleven faculties is called the gross body (sthūla-deha).
Regarding these eight types of existence (*bhava*) and the two entities of the perfumed (*vāsanā*), which arises first:
do the eight existences come first, or do the two entities come first?
The answer is that both explanations clarify that there is no priority or sequence between the eight existences and the two entities.
They must be associated and co-arise,
just as fire and heat cannot be separated from one another,
or like the two horns of an ox, which necessarily arise together.
The same applies to the existence (bhava) and its essential characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
When there is the self-nature (svabhāva), the cognition (buddhi), the conceit (māna), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra), these eight must necessarily be present.
Within existence, there are four types.
If these four dharmas did not exist, then there would be four [others];
dharma and non-dharma can never be separated from one another.
These are born of one's parents.
The coarse body is likewise;
its essential nature is likewise.
It is determined that it cannot be separated from the eight [consciousnesses].
The third existence is called the existence of sentient beings (*saṃjñin*), as stated in the verse:
"In the heavenly realm there are eight divisions; in the animal realm there are five divisions."
The human realm consists of only one birth; briefly termed "the birth of sentient beings.
The heavenly realms consist of eight divisions:
first, the birth of the Brahma Kings.
Second, the birth of the lords of the world;
third, the birth of the celestial emperors;
fourth, the birth of the gandharvas.
Fifth, birth as an asura;
sixth, birth as a yakṣa;
seventh, birth as a rākṣasa.
The eight sand-spirits are born there.
Regarding the five types of birth within the animal realm:
the first is birth from feet.
Second, birth by flying;
third, birth by crawling on the chest;
fourth, birth from side-slipping forms.
There are five types of non-arising births.
Regarding the human realm having only one type of birth:
this is because the human realm consists of only a single class.
It is said that there are three kinds of sentient beings:
namely, the triad of devas, animals, and humans; and the triad of conditioned existence (saṃskṛta) according to its characteristics.
An outsider asks:
Among the three worlds, what increases most in which place?
Answering in verse:
In the upper realms, joy and pleasure abound; In the root [realm], the darkness of delusion is most prevalent.
Those born in the intermediate [heavens] have much sorrow and suffering; those beginning with the Brahma-world and ending with the Peak of Existence have increasingly more joy and bliss,
such that in the Brahma-abodes, joy and bliss are most abundant.
This [realm] also possesses the darkness of sorrow,
for it is overwhelmed and oppressed by the joy and pleasure [of the higher realms].
The Brahmā and other devas experience much joy and pleasure.
Regarding those in whom delusion and darkness abound from birth:
this refers to beings such as animals, birds, and even those born from pillars and the like, who do not engage in [right] conduct.
Among these, darkness and delusion are predominant.
These beings also possess sorrow and joy;
because they are oppressed and overcome by darkness and delusion,
animals and others abound in such darkness and delusion.
Those born from roots are born from three [factors].
Because they are the most inferior, they are called "roots.
Those born from moisture experience much sorrow and suffering.
In human life, sorrow and suffering predominate;
there is also joy, yet it is obscured by ignorance.
Because sorrow is so prevalent, [it is not perceived].
Because they are oppressed by the darkness of joy,
humans have much sorrow and suffering;
the human realm is called the "middle."
Because it stands in the midst of the three paths,
why is the final birth called a "pillar"?
This refers to grasses, trees, mountains, stones, and so forth.
Because the three worlds are supported by these, they are called "pillars.
Such characteristics as these give rise to birth; once sentient beings have been born, it is fully explained that these three births constitute their own nature.
Because it is produced by nature,
its essential function is already fulfilled;
that is to say, the production of the world and the attainment of liberation.
The opponent says:
Among those in the three worlds—humans, devas, and animals—who experiences pleasure and pain?
Is it experienced as having self-nature (*svabhāva*)?
If it is for the sake of experiencing the five objects of consciousness up to the eleven faculties and so forth,
this is the experience of the "person-self" (pudgala-ātman).
In response, he says in verse:

Regarding the suffering of old age and death herein: only a person of wisdom can accept it, for its essential characteristics have not yet been transcended; therefore, it is briefly described as suffering.
As for "only a person of wisdom can accept the suffering of old age and death herein": [it refers to one who understands the nature of phenomena].
Within the three worlds there is suffering,
which is wrought by this old age:
the skin becomes wrinkled, the hair turns white and falls out, the breath becomes wheezing, one must lean on a staff, and one is held in contempt by friends and kin.
Such sufferings as these all arise because of old age.
As for the suffering of death:
there are those who have attained the eight masteries.
Sometimes they perceive five subtle particles,
and sometimes they perceive coarse particles;
such a person, at the point of death—
Recorded by Yama, one undergoes suffering therein called the "suffering of death.
Furthermore, there are three types of suffering during the intermediate period.
The wise are able to accept these three kinds of suffering:
intrinsic nature and the coarse body;
because they lack wisdom, the ignorant are unable to accept them.
Therefore, it is said that human suffering is not suffering by its own nature (svabhāva).
An opponent asks:
For how long does a person experience this suffering?
The answer is:
Because its essential nature and characteristics have not yet been separated [from suffering], it is briefly described as suffering.
Because one has not yet been separated from the coarse and subtle bodily sufferings characterized by the great elements and so forth,
and because one has not yet been separated from transmigrating within the world with this coarse body,
at such a time, the person and the self undergo suffering.
If the subtle and the coarse are separated from one another,
the person and the self are immediately liberated.
When liberation occurs, such sufferings as these are ultimately not experienced.
If one has not yet abandoned the subtle and coarse characteristics,
then one cannot attain liberation from suffering;
therefore, the subtle and coarse characteristics are briefly explained as being suffering.
The opponent asks:
"Is this the only matter regarding intrinsic nature, or is there more?
He replies with a verse:

The nature of things is thus: for those who have attained liberation from the three realms through awakening and the five great elements, their own nature of things is such that they act for others just as they act for themselves.
"Awakening and the five great elements" refers to this very nature of things.
What is the meaning of this verse?
It refers to the meaning of the seventy verses,
whose characteristics have already been fully established.
Why is this so? Because two aspects of intrinsic nature have been manifested:
first, the sequential arising of birth and death.
May I be associated with the dust of the three worlds so that [the evolutes] arise in succession: first consciousness arises;
from consciousness arises ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra); from ego-consciousness arise the five subtle elements (tanmātra).
From the five subtle elements (tanmātra) arise the eleven faculties and the five gross elements.
These twenty-three factors, beginning with the body and cognition, [constitute the manifest world].
The five great elements are placed last. Second,
regarding liberation from the three realms of existence, one who treats others as oneself acts for the sake of liberating the self and the personhood within the heavenly realms,
as well as the self and the personhood within the human and animal realms.
The eight [limbs] are accomplished in succession.
Now, seeing the self-nature within the midst of the self,
these two serve only others and not oneself.
For example, it is like a person who performs the duties of a friend but does not perform his own duty.
In this way, intrinsic nature (svabhāva) only performs the work of others and has no work for itself.
The opponent says:
You claim that once the self-nature has performed the functions of a person and a self, one then becomes free from the self;
yet this self-nature is devoid of cognition,
whereas only the person and the self possess cognition.
How does mental attention cause others to engage with sense objects,
to revolve through the three worlds,
and subsequently attain liberation?
If one holds the view that this is not a state of ignorance,
the answer is:
one has already seen that ignorance is like objects having conjunction and disjunction.
As it is said in verse:
"Just as for the sake of nourishing a calf, Ignorance is transformed into milk;
So too is the nature of ignorance For the sake of liberating the person and the self."
It is for the sake of increasing the ignorance of the calf so that it may be transformed into milk;
just as in the world, when ignorant grass and water are consumed by the cow,
they should nourish the calf.
If one were to maintain such a calculation,
it would be possible to turn [the milk] into curd within a single year;
once the calf has grown up...
Once the cow has finished eating the grass, it then consumes water and grass,
which do not transform into milk.

As for the statement that "the nature of ignorance is likewise for the sake of liberating the person and the self," this means that the very nature of such ignorance performs the function of the self to bring about liberation,
whether through conjunction or separation.
Once separated, they do not reunite.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"In order to avoid instability, it is like worldly affairs."
In order that I may attain liberation, [I shall practice] even when not understanding the task;
likewise, in order to abandon instability, just as worldly people act, so too should one act when the mind is unstable,
like those in the world whose minds are unsettled.
Coming and going between them is for the sake of abandoning instability.
If one thinks, "May I be liberated," yet the matter remains unresolved, it is likewise so;
because of the self, there is instability by its very nature.
The tasks that must be performed for the sake of the Puruṣa are two:
first, the grasping of objects such as sound, and second, the grasping of the three guṇas.
Once instability has been removed from between the Puruṣa and the intellect (buddhi), [these tasks are accomplished].
Finally, they attain dissociation.
"Non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*) is a specific designation for its own nature,
because it has already transcended the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, it is also called "obscure" (mīng).
How is this known?
